utterances.text: Yes, you may put your questions, Mr. Milosevic, and bear in mind we're about 15 minutes from today's break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, but I will not be able to finish the examination-in-chief today, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in order to save time, could you please just quote the middle paragraph, the 16th of January. What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of January, 1999. "Today there were also conflicts in Petrovo and in Racak."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you're being asked to slow down by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "There were conflicts in Petrovo and in Racak today as well. The conflicts were very fierce from the morning until the evening. The enemy tried to enter the village in order to take the massacred corpses from the previous day. Almost the entire unit was there. Our positions were together with Guri's soldiers. On that day we repelled the Serb forces three times and incurred losses in their ranks through war operations and in the infantry."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he says today also there were conflicts in Petrovo and Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he says what they informed their battalion, to go there. They say that Guri units were there, that is to say the others that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are not going to deal with the item on 15th of January, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him to read the -- the middle part, where it says, "Today as well there were conflicts in Petrovo and Racak." So that means that there is repetition, meaning that there had been conflicts previously, also on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read the 15th.

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Friday, the 15th of January. They informed us from the battalion to get ready and to go to our positions. After 15 minutes of reconnaissance, we went back to base. When we went to barracks, we saw that some wounded had already been brought in from Petrovo and Racak. We asked to be transferred by car to the places where the conflicts were taking place. We took two vehicles to Petrovo Selo. We asked the local people about the positions of our soldiers. We joined the soldiers of the unit Guri (stone) Baskim, Zija, Ibis, Saip, Bekim, Hazir, Xhevet, Betim, Amir, Husen, Besim Salja were there. At that moment, the jeep of commander Abi arrived. Commanders Guri and Abi again wanted to attack but they didn't do that because the OSCE mission was present. We placed mortars in order to attack, but the enemy withdrew. Our positions were 3 to 500 metres away from the enemy. When we returned to Guri with Hamdija, we took three wounded soldiers from Racak, put them in the konbi van and drove them to the hospital in Pagarusa. We took this road and went back to our base at 4.30."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask something. When you read that at the beginning, the first three or four lines, you referred to wounded from Petrovo and Racak. Is that what it actually says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It actually says Recani, but it wasn't very legible. So these are wounded from Petrovo and Recani, which is about 50 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wasn't Racak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, at the very end, in the last three sentence -- last three lines, does it say, "When we returned to Guri with Hamdija, we took three wounded soldiers from Racak"?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say Racak or something else?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the last but one line here in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was the word "soldier" used here?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 16th, it says: "Today as well there were conflicts in Petrovo and in Racak." So what does this say, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that -- it shows that the terrorists knew that there was an action under way and that they were organising themselves in order to assist the terrorists who were already in Racak. Baskim Ndrecaj was commander of a special unit that was stationed in Budakovo. Budakovo, Racak, Luzak. That's about ten kilometres. It's a bad road, bad roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think that we have concluded this particular topic now. Let's move on to the next one, Mr. Janicevic. In addition to the group of terrorists who called themselves the 161st Brigade of the KLA, you mentioned the 162nd Brigade. In which area did it operate?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was its headquarters in the area too?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the headquarters of this terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters were in the village of Ivaja, municipality of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was commander of that staff?

utterances.speaker: BOGOLJUB JANICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibri Ilazi [phoen], nickname I cannot remember. Ilazi, from Kacanik, a former --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll have to break here. Mr. Nice wanted five minutes to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't concern this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't concern this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Janicevic, you may leave and return on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I put on the record something that is of concern arising from yesterday's evidence where the accused, in my respectful submission to the Chamber, behaved improperly, and for a clear oblique purpose that he may indeed in part have achieved. It was in the re-examination of the witness where he introduced a video of Lord Ashdown. It was introduced all of a piece without any careful analysis of what it showed. It was clearly designed to suggest that it was all connected, and it was then followed by a question that His Honour Judge Bonomy recognised was ill-founded, where he suggested that Lord Ashdown had expressed that it was a scandal for the people to whom he was talking, who he sought to identify clearly with the KLA, had such poor quality weapons. Now, we put up in this Chamber with, so far as I'm concerned, recurring abuse by this accused of a personal nature. We put up with things being said by him about people, one type and another, that would never be allowed if he were a qualified and proper advocate. We put up with it, I suppose, simply to allow the case to go on. But these things can have serious effects, and I've been contacted by Lord Ashdown who, of course, holds an extremely important international public office and who observes that what the accused did yesterday achieves effect on the ground in adverse and potentially serious publicity, at which the accused is clearly aiming. And I must put on the record just a couple of things about that video that was played yesterday. First, there was, of course, a clear separation between the people who were dressed in KLA uniforms and the people who were producing weapons that Lord Ashdown was looking at. There was no identity between the KLA people and the people showing the weapons. Second, Lord Ashdown gave evidence about this in detail in this court a couple of years ago, and as to the examination of the weapons, he explained what account was given to him by the villagers who produced those weapons to him. Third, insofar as the people shown in that third clip of the composite video were young men, it's a matter he has dealt with in detail at page 286 of the second volume of his diaries. And lest there be any suggestion of partiality by Lord Ashdown, if the accused had had the decency, before trying to put in the clip for the purpose he plainly sought, if he'd had the decency to review Lord Ashdown's book carefully, he would have found that on a footnote not only did Lord Ashdown give the account that was given to him of why those weapons were being produced, but he also set out how his colleague Brian Donnelly had suspicions that the people he had been speaking to were introduced to him by a member of the KLA. So that in fact what was presented yesterday and then summarised in a quite improper question was something that has always been the testimony of Lord Ashdown and that he has published at an earlier date in detail and in full. Now, the consequences of this type of action by this accused we always hope will not be serious. Nevertheless, when dealing with somebody like Lord Ashdown, they may have consequences, and it's only right that the matter should be put right on the record as soon as possible. I should say that Lord Ashdown is absolutely at your disposal to give further evidence, if you wish, on the questions that have been raised by recent witnesses as to his position. Thank you for letting me make that plain. There's one other point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other point. We have prepared these Rules of Service that have been referred to. They're not an exhibit at the moment. They are a voluminous document, but nevertheless it seemed prudent to produce them in both languages. Now, they are available. We can bring them in and out on the trolly every day but the trollies sometimes get rather full. If the Chamber would like them, we can distribute them now. If not, we'll take them back and store them, but they are now available. And I mention that because it was the Chamber itself that raised at some stage the question of these Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you elaborate more on the third point, which I didn't follow before, in relation to Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His availability to come back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the reference to colleague Brian Donnelly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 286.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. He relates -- and his entire diaries are not before you. He relates in his book, as he related to us, the explanation that was given to him about the weapons that were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His book, you mean Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown's book. His diary. His book is called "Diary," I think. It's volume 2 of that. And he related to us exactly the same way as he relates in his book the account given for the production of weapons, that it was explained to him, were weapons that had to be produced to the JNA by the KLA and he explains the, as he described it in the words of the others, the corrupt trade that that constituted. But the person who took them to this place, described as a garage owner, was a person who features a little earlier in Lord Ashdown's narrative in the same chapter, and as a matter of complete fairness, he records in what is footnote 1 to this particular part of his diaries, that Brian Donnelly, who was his colleague at the time, or his fellow on this particular journey, has since told him that he strongly suspected this man was in fact KLA. So that everything that we've seen was the subject of evidence by Lord Ashdown and has been contemporaneously and fully recorded by him, and to present it in some way as it was done yesterday was extremely unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has had the occasion previously to reproach you for misusing the proceedings. The proceedings are not to be used for non-forensic purposes. Sometimes you do it and it is not picked up. Sometimes do you it and it is picked up, but in any event, I want to stress that the proceedings are not to be used and will not be allowed to be used for non-forensic purposes. We will adjourn until -- and I thank Mr. Nice for the clarification. We will adjourn until 9.00 a.m. on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I consider that your acceptance of the explanation given by Mr. Nice is -- lacks objectivity because the film speaks for itself. You can see people wearing KLA uniforms on the film, and you can see that one by one, taken in order, he is trying out the rifles and categorising them. Ashdown, I mean. If that was his role in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are going to adjourn until Monday. I thought you had something --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I take one minute of your time? Because the accused is doing exactly what he did yesterday, and it is wickedly intended. The film and the book make it absolutely plain that Lord Ashdown met some members of the KLA at the side of the road and spoke to them, the young men in uniform. He makes it plain that he then went elsewhere, as indeed the video shows. He makes it plain that the next set of people he spoke to, and where he was seen looking at guns that had been collected, were different and differently introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the evidence is there before us. We will adjourn until 9.00 a.m. on Monday.
